abstract: Continuous fibre-reinforced nylon produced by fused filament fabrication (FFF) offers great potential for lightweight structural applications; however, process-induced defects such as porosity, fibre misalignment and inter-bead discontinuities can significantly reduce compressive performance. This study investigates the role of these microstructural features in governing damage evolution and collapse in continuous carbon fibre-reinforced (CFRP) and glass fibre-reinforced (GFRP) nylon under uniaxial compression using in-situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (XCT). XCT scans recorded before and after compression are analysed using a deep learning-based segmentation framework to quantify phase fractions, fibre orientation and void morphology. CFRP exhibits higher void content (11%–12%) and lower fibre volume fractions (30%–33%) than GFRP with approx. 70% and 50% of fibres oriented within 2.5° of the extrusion direction. For both CFRP samples and one GFRP sample, kinking was observed out-of-plane of the printed layers, accompanied by fibre fracture and delamination. In the other case, the GFRP exhibited more distributed deformation characterised by fibre reorientation, bending instability and interlaminar damage. This was ascribed to a reduction in lateral constraint arising from interlaminar voids, but the lower degree of fibre alignment for that sample may also contribute. These results show how compressive failure in continuous-fibre FFF composites is controlled by the coupled interactions between fibre architecture, void morphology and nonuniform local stress field, providing a basis for microstructure-informed process optimisation and improved structural performance.

abstract: Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is a widely used 3D printing method due to its low cost, material versatility, and design flexibility. However, FDM-printed parts often suffer from poor mechanical strength caused by weak bonding between layers. Coating filaments with graphene oxide (GO) has been shown to improve these mechanical properties. In this study, ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used to investigate how GO coatings enhance interfacial strength in FDM printing. The results show that the degree of GO oxidation, the covalent bonding rate and spatial distribution of interfacial bonding sites significantly affect the bonding strength between layers. Using the Taguchi method, the theoretical optimized molecular-scale interfacial strength was predicted to reach ∼40.54 GPa under the simulated conditions. Furthermore, an idealized interface with uniformly distributed covalent bonding sites was predicted to achieve a theoretical upper-bound interfacial strength, corresponding to a ∼65.46% improvement over the optimized configuration. The simulation results qualitatively reproduce the experimental strengthening trend, providing molecular-scale insights into interfacial reinforcement mechanisms and a rational basis for optimizing GO coating characteristics and printing parameters to enhance the mechanical performance of FDM-printed parts.

abstract: Brick-and-mortar carbon fibre structures have attracted considerable attention owing to their reliable mechanical performance, including high damage tolerance, multiple energy dissipation mechanisms and the potential to use carbon fibre scraps instead of pristine carbon fibre prepregs. Although numerous studies have focused on thermoset matrix systems, their behaviour under specific loading conditions, particularly Mode I and Mode II interlaminar fracture, remains unclear. To address this gap, the present study investigated the mechanical behaviour of brick-and-mortar laminates manually fabricated from carbon fibre/poly-ether-ether-ketone tapes with brick lengths of 50, 25 and 10 mm. Tensile, Mode I interlaminar fracture and Mode II interlaminar fracture tests were conducted to evaluate the mechanical response of the laminates. The brick-and-mortar structure retained approximately 88% of the stiffness of the continuous laminate, whereas the tensile strength decreased notably from 1860 MPa for the continuous laminate to 960 MPa for the strongest discontinuous configuration, corresponding to a brick length of 25 mm. In Mode I, the average fracture toughness was 1.75 kJ/m 2 for the 25-mm brick-length sample, compared with 1.76 kJ/m 2 for the continuous configuration. In Mode II, the fracture toughness increased by 33% for the 10-mm brick-length samples, reaching 5.10 kJ/m 2 compared with 3.83 kJ/m 2 for the continuous samples. Numerical simulations were performed to examine the underlying failure mechanisms, and the results demonstrated good agreement with the experimental observations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of brick-and-mortar configurations for thermoplastic composite structures.

abstract: Recent advancements in deep learning offer considerable potential for automated composite damage recognition. However, limited annotated datasets and complex material microstructures challenge pixel-level characterization of local damage mechanisms, while existing approaches provide limited integration of segmentation outputs with quantitative damage assessment. A deep learning-based convolutional neural network was integrated with digital imaging and automated crack counting algorithms to characterize damage in unidirectional non-crimp fabric glass fiber-reinforced reactive thermoplastic cross-ply laminates. Microscopic images of damage-containing material samples obtained in previous work were preprocessed and annotated with six feature-related classes for model training and testing. A U-Net architecture incorporating skip connections, dropout, and a weighted Dice loss function was employed to segment material features and damage. Results showed that smaller batch sizes produced the lowest weighted Dice loss and the highest Dice coefficients. Notably, the Dice coefficient improved significantly from ∼0.736 with equal class weights to ∼0.840 with optimized class weights, representing a 14.1% increase in the prediction accuracy of 90° tow cracks (the dominant damage mechanism). A controlled factorial ablation study further evaluated key model components across eight configurations and three random seeds. Removing skip connections from the full model reduced the mean Dice coefficient by approximately 51.6%, demonstrating their importance for multi-class segmentation. The trained model demonstrated a strong capability to identify damage initiation, progression, and interaction, and was integrated with automated crack counting algorithms for quantitative damage assessment. The resulting damage metrics could support analytical damage-mechanics models for predicting stiffness degradation and informing structural health monitoring and maintenance planning.

abstract: This study develops and experimentally validates a computationally efficient finite element model for predicting the mechanical response of 3D-printed continuous carbon-fibre-reinforced nylon laminates under tensile and shear-dominated loading conditions. The printed composite is represented within an equivalent single-layer formulation using homogenised theoretical plies. The constitutive formulation accounts explicitly for nonlinear transverse tensile and in-plane shear behaviour. Damage initiation is evaluated using the Hashin criterion. Depending on the identified failure mechanism, selective degradation of the relevant stiffness components is applied. For matrix-dominated failure modes, the formulation further distinguishes between transverse-tension- and shear-dominated failure and employs an additional strain-threshold criterion to govern degradation activation. Linear elastic, nonlinear constitutive and damage-related material parameters were identified from tensile tests on [0°] 4 , [90°] 4 and balanced [45°/-45°] s laminates. The parameter governing mixed transverse-tension/shear matrix failure was calibrated using the [45°] 4 configuration. The model was validated without further parameter adjustment using [0°/90°] s , [15°/-75°] s and [30°/-60°] s tensile and V-notched Iosipescu specimens. The consistency of the in-plane shear modulus identified from the balanced [45°/-45°] s laminate was verified using the [45°] 4 and V-notched Iosipescu configurations. Mechanical extensometers, strain gauges and digital image correlation provided the global stress-strain responses and local strain fields used for model identification and validation, confirming that characterisation procedures commonly employed for conventional composite laminates remain applicable to the investigated 3D-printed material. Compared with the built-in Abaqus Hashin damage model incorporating the experimentally observed nonlinear transverse-tension and in-plane shear constitutive relations, the proposed formulation provided more accurate predictions of the mechanical response of the investigated laminates.

abstract: In this study, two invariant-based failure criteria are proposed to predict failure of a unidirectional non-crimp fabric (UD-NCF) carbon fiber/epoxy composite. Three different failure modes, namely matrix failure, fiber tensile failure, and fiber compressive failure, are considered. The matrix failure functions are based on linear and quadratic transversely isotropic stress-invariants, while fiber failure is evaluated with a maximum stress criterion for tension and an adapted kinking criterion for compression. The main advantages of the invariant-based criteria are fewer required experiments for calibration and minimal computational effort in comparison with fracture plane-based criteria. Moreover, the chosen mathematical formulation ensures a non-negative Hessian and decoupled tensile and compressive behaviour. Furthermore, the strain rate dependency of the investigated UD-NCF composite is incorporated using empirical relations defined in previous work by the authors. For validation purposes, off-axis tests are performed at quasi-static and high strain rates. Overall, the observed agreement with experimental data presented here as well as from literature is excellent, highlighting the feasibility of the proposed criteria for design of UD-NCF composite structures.

title: MOF-on-MOF-derived GC/Co@CNTs with multiscale heterostructures for enhanced microwave absorption
abstract: Metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived electromagnetic wave absorption have attracted considerable interest because of their tunable composition, rich porosity, and structural versatility. However, conventional single-MOF-derived materials often have limited metallic components and single-dimensional structures, which hinder the simultaneous optimization of electromagnetic wave absorption performance. In this work, a ZIF-L@ZIF-67 precursor with a MOF-on-MOF architecture was designed. Through high-temperature pyrolysis, it was converted into Graphitized carbon/Co nanoparticles@carbon nanotubes (GC/Co@CNTs) composites composed of two-dimensional graphitized carbon, one-dimensional carbon nanotubes, and zero-dimensional Co nanoparticles. By tuning the pyrolysis temperature, the magnetic-dielectric response of the materials was effectively regulated. The minimum reflection loss reached −69.4 dB at a thickness of 1.85 mm, while an effective absorption bandwidth of 6.04 GHz at a thickness of 2.00 mm was obtained at 800 °C. During pyrolysis, the in-situ formation of a conductive carbon network, magnetic Co nanoparticles, and abundant heterogeneous interfaces synergistically promoted conduction loss, magnetic loss, and interfacial polarization. As a result, the electromagnetic attenuation capability of the composites was significantly improved. This study highlights the considerable promise of MOF-on-MOF-derived architectures for electromagnetic wave absorption and offers a viable structural engineering strategy for the development of next-generation microwave absorbers.

abstract: This work compares self-heating and its influence on fatigue strength and life of a quasi-isotropic CF-PAEK laminate with that of an orthotropic CF-PEKK laminate using thermographic approaches at low ( ≤ 40 Hz) and ultrasonic frequencies ( ≈ 20 kHz). The fatigue strengths were found to be approximately 47.9 MPa for CF-PAEK and 50.0 MPa for CF-PEKK at a low frequency of 40 Hz. At a cyclic frequency of 20 kHz, fatigue strength decreased by approximately 12% and 16%, respectively, reaching a value of 42 MPa for the CF-PAEK and CF-PEKK laminates. The total heat dissipation rates escalated from an order of magnitude of 10 5 J m − 3 s −1 at low to about 1 0 6 J m − 3 s − 1 at ultrasonic frequencies. A critical aspect of this work is the separation of damage-related heat dissipation rate from reversible internal friction in order to use it as a reliable physical indicator to characterize self-heating in polymer matrix composites (PMCs). The damage-related heat dissipation rate was higher for the CF-PAEK laminate under low frequency cyclic loading, leading to shorter fatigue lives in the high-cycle fatigue regime. In the very high-cycle fatigue regime, comparable damage-related heat dissipation rates between CF-PAEK and CF-PEKK laminates lead to comparable fatigue lives. These results, alongside literature data on the self-heating of PMCs with different fiber orientations, show that a major portion of the self-heating temperature rise associated with high heat-dissipation rates for off-axis fiber orientations under shear-dominated loading can be primarily attributed to contributions from internal friction.

abstract: It is well known that Bouligand structures derive their impact tolerance from low-pitch helicoidal fibre architectures that steer cracks and regulate damage growth. This study examines the low-velocity impact response of continuous aramid fibre-reinforced nylon composites manufactured by dual-extrusion fused filament fabrication (FFF) with pitch angles of 5°, 10°, 20°, and 45°. Instrumented impact testing is combined with post-mortem high-resolution X-ray computed tomography (XCT) to characterise how pitch angle influences impact response and damage topology. In particular, we use a DNN-assisted segmentation framework to classify through-thickness cracking, delamination, and filament fracture. While previous studies have demonstrated the beneficial influence of low-pitch Bouligand architectures on impact resistance, the present work provides volumetric quantification of intralaminar cracking, delamination, and filament fracture within continuous-fibre FFF Bouligand structures, revealing how their interaction evolves with pitch angle. The results show that the lowest-pitch laminate exhibits the highest peak load and absorbed energy, while low-pitch architectures also promote more distributed damage and suppress filament fracture.

abstract: Braid angle is a key design variable for braided composite tubes, yet its role in governing damage evolution in multilayer tubular architectures under torsion remains insufficiently understood. Here, time-resolved in-situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT) has been used to investigate the torsional behaviour of double-layer 1/1 braided CFRP tubes with braid angles of 30° (DL30), 45° (DL45) and 60° (DL60). Increasing braid angle progressively increased wall thickness and tow crimp, while the effective fibre volume fraction varied only modestly and non-monotonically. These architectural changes produced distinct mechanical responses: DL45 and DL60 exhibit higher tube-level torsional stiffness whereas DL30 displays the highest shear modulus and torsional strength. Damage accumulation is strongly braid-angle dependent. At higher strain levels, intra-tow cracking, inter-tow debonding and inter-laminar debonding all markedly reduce as braid angle increases. The predominant damage mechanism also changes: DL30 develops a rapidly connected damage network (intra-tow cracking and inter-tow/laminar debonding) promoting microscale fibre kinking/buckling and further fibre breakage, leading to an abrupt post-peak loss of strength; DL45 showed more distributed damage accumulation and the highest post-peak strength; while DL60 exhibited delayed, weakly connected damage evolution with the lowest overall level of damage accumulation. These results suggest that angle-graded multilayer designs could combine lower-angle regions for reduced tow crimp, higher shear modulus and strength, with intermediate or higher-angle regions for damage suppression and stable post-peak performance.

abstract: This paper presents the first experimental and numerical investigation to explore the effect of hybridisation of 0° plies in a cross-ply laminate on the failure response of open-hole composites in compression. In this study, open hole compression (OHC) tests are conducted in accordance with the ASTM D6484 test standard. A three-dimensional ply-by-ply finite element model (FEA) employing cohesive layers, and Hashin and Quads damage criteria, was created to perform the analysis. The effect of varying the position of the 0° glass fibre ply within the stacking sequence was explored. Experimentally, the failure sequences were investigated via Digital Image Correlation (DIC) to detect the initiation and propagation of the damage events on the surface. Post-mortem X-ray computed tomography (CT) was undertaken to identify the three-dimensional damage morphology and to compare the spatial distribution of damage modes between the different configurations. Among the configurations investigated, we identified a particular hybrid configuration maintained an OHC strength comparable to that of the unhybridised carbon-fibre baseline while increasing the displacement at failure by 13.9%. This improvement is associated with the overall H3 laminate architecture, including the position of the glass plies, the distribution of local sublaminate stiffness, and the arrangement of ply interfaces. The FEA results were in good agreement with the experimental results and helps to understand failure mechanism. This work illustrates the key benefit of optimised ply hybridisation when aiming to maximise the global compressive strength response at the structural detail level.

abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates with full-revolution bio-inspired helicoidal layups have demonstrated outstanding impact resistance and out-of-plane strength. However, as most aerospace applications demand CFRP laminates with high mechanical performance along the primary in-plane loading direction, a segmented Directional-Biased-Helicoidal (DBH) laminate that offers superior in-plane strength, stiffness, and Compression-After-Impact (CAI) strength along one direction is more practical than conventional full-revolution helicoidal laminates. This study investigates the out-of-plane and CAI performance of DBH laminates to assess their potential in aerospace applications. The results show that the spiraling matrix split damage developed in DBH laminates can effectively reduce fiber fracture and increase their out-of-plane peak load between 24% and 33.6% compared to the conventional directional biased quadriaxial (Quad) laminate. Under impact loading, unlike conventional quasi-isotropic (QI) laminates, delaminations in Quad laminates tend to concentrate and grow excessively at a few interfaces due to stiffness mismatch between ply clusters. In contrast DBH layups can restrict such extensive delamination formation. The experimental result shows that the CAI strength (based on ASTM D7137/D7137M test standard) of the DBH laminate with an inter-ply angle of 30 o outperforms the Quad counterpart by a remarkable 35.3%. More surprisingly, further experiments showed that the CAI strength of the full-revolution helicoidal laminate with the same inter-ply angle was 23.2% lower than one of its QI counterparts. The impact-induced damage patterns and CAI performance of these laminates were investigated with the aid of CT scanning and numerical simulation.
